abstract: Network intrusion detection systems (IDS) serve as critical components in modern cybersecurity infrastructure, providing real-time monitoring and classification of network traffic to identify potential security threats. This study presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of machine learning approaches for binary network intrusion classification using the NSL-KDD benchmark dataset, which contains 63,280 training and 22,544 test samples across 121 features. Three students independently investigated different algorithm families: Ensemble Methods (BaggingClassifier with 150 decision tree estimators), Non-Linear Methods (DecisionTreeClassifier with depth-20 constraint), and Support Vector Methods (RidgeClassifier with L2 regularization). The experimental methodology employed 5-fold stratified cross-validation, systematic hyperparameter optimization, bootstrap-based bias-variance decomposition, and comprehensive multi-metric evaluation including Balanced Accuracy, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), Attack Detection Rate, and False Alarm Rate. Results demonstrate clear performance stratification: the BaggingClassifier achieved the highest performance with 91.60% balanced accuracy, 0.8244 MCC, 87.20% attack detection rate, and only 4.00% false alarm rate. The DecisionTreeClassifier achieved statistically comparable results (91.19% balanced accuracy, 0.8160 MCC) while offering interpretability advantages. The RidgeClassifier substantially underperformed (79.18% balanced accuracy, 0.5894 MCC), with bias-variance decomposition confirming fundamental underfitting (bias=0.2276) due to linear separability limitations. The study contributes empirical benchmarks for NSL-KDD classification, demonstrates the value of bias-variance analysis for understanding classifier behavior, and provides actionable guidance for practitioners: non-linear methods are essential for effective intrusion detection, appropriate metrics (balanced accuracy, MCC) are critical for imbalanced datasets, and model selection should consider the accuracy-interpretability-efficiency tradeoff. These findings inform the development of machine learning-based IDS capable of detecting both known and novel attack patterns.
